item.title: Board certification: what every new Florida condo and HOA director has to finish
item.description: Issue #2: the training rules for new directors and DBPR's latest rule moves
item.content:encoded:
Informational, not legal advice. This newsletter summarizes Florida statutes and official sources in plain English. It isn't legal advice and doesn't create an attorney-client relationship. Your declaration, bylaws and specific facts matter. For decisions affecting your association, consult a Florida-licensed attorney or the DBPR Division of Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes. We're nonpartisan, take no position on legislation, and endorse no candidates.

Last week we promised to cover the education every new director has to complete. That's below, along with the rule changes the Division has moved on this month.

Last issue

Issue #1 covered where Florida condo and HOA law stands after the 2026 session: HB 657 died in the Senate, while HB 797 and HB 803 took effect July 1. It also walked through how owners can attend and speak at board meetings and the condo election calendar. Read Issue #1.

Subscribe to the Condo Brief: get each issue free in your inbox. Subscribe at condohoabrief.com/subscribe.

1. New laws, rules & deadlines (plain English)

The Division's reserve rule took effect, and it's already being amended again. - The revised Rule 61B-22.005 (Reserves) took effect October 4, 2026. It implements the SIRS and reserve-funding sections of the condo statute (rule history, Florida Administrative Register). - On October 22, 2026, the Division published a new proposed amendment to the same rule. Its stated purpose is to clarify language about adjustments to the annual reserve funding amount and about changes between pooled and straight-line reserve accounting (FAR Vol. 52/206). It's a proposal, not yet law. If your board is finalizing a 2027 budget now, ask your manager or attorney whether it affects you.

Condo meeting rule: revised, still proposed. - On October 16, 2026, the Division published a notice of change to proposed Rule 61B-23.001, the rule on board and committee meetings (FAR Vol. 52/202). - The original July proposal said it would update the rule and implement s. 718.112(2), F.S. (from HB 913), including the definition of "committee meeting" and the use of video and audio meetings (rule history). - The rule in force today is still the 1999 version. Nothing changes for your meetings until a final rule is adopted and takes effect.

2. Explainer: board certification, condo vs. HOA

Condo directors (Chapter 718) — s. 718.112(2)(d), F.S. - Every newly elected or appointed director must give the association secretary two things: a written certification that they've read the declaration, articles, bylaws and current written policies, and an educational certificate. - Timing: within 1 year before or 90 days after election or appointment. - The course: at least 4 hours, from the Division or a Division-approved provider. It must cover milestone inspections, SIRS, elections, recordkeeping, financial literacy and transparency, fines, and notice and meeting rules. - How long it lasts: 7 years, as long as the director serves without interruption. - Every year after: at least 1 hour of continuing education on recent changes to Chapter 718 and its rules. - If you miss it: you're suspended from the board until you comply. The board may temporarily fill the seat. Board actions stay valid even if a certificate isn't on file. - The secretary keeps the certificates for owners to inspect for 7 years after election or the length of uninterrupted tenure, whichever is longer.

HOA directors (Chapter 720) — s. 720.3033(1), F.S. - New directors must submit a certificate from a department-approved education provider within 90 days after election or appointment. - The course must include financial literacy and transparency, recordkeeping, levying of fines, and notice and meeting requirements. - The certificate is valid for up to 4 years, and the new-director course must be repeated at least every 4 years. - Annual continuing education: at least 4 hours for associations with fewer than 2,500 parcels, and 8 hours for 2,500 parcels or more. - If you miss it: suspended until you comply. The HOA keeps certificates for members to inspect for 5 years.

Cost: the Division offers a free Board Member Certification course in English and Spanish (DBPR press releases).

Condo (718) HOA (720)
Deadline 1 yr before to 90 days after 90 days after
Initial course 4+ hours Department-approved curriculum
Valid for 7 years Up to 4 years
Annual CE 1 hour 4 or 8 hours
Records kept 7 yrs or tenure 5 years

3. How to get involved: check your board's certificates

Certificates are association records owners and members can ask to inspect (s. 718.112(2)(d); s. 720.3033(1)(c)). This week's action: ask your association's secretary or manager whether each current director's certificate is on file, and note when the next annual continuing-education deadline falls.

Next issue: the director conflict-of-interest rules, including how HB 797 changed what HOA boards must do (s. 720.3033(2)).

4. Florida sponsor

item.title: Where Florida condo & HOA law stands after the 2026 session
item.description: Issue #1: what changed, what died, and the deadlines still ahead
item.content:encoded:
Informational, not legal advice. This newsletter summarizes Florida statutes and official sources in plain English. It is not legal advice and does not create an attorney-client relationship. Your declaration, bylaws and specific facts matter. For decisions affecting your association, consult a Florida-licensed attorney or the DBPR Division of Condominiums, Timeshares and Mobile Homes. We are nonpartisan, take no position on legislation, and endorse no candidates.

Welcome to the first issue. Every week we'll cover what changed, what's due, and how owners, board members and managers can take part in their communities, for condos (Chapter 718) and HOAs (Chapter 720) alike.

1. New laws, rules & deadlines (plain English)

The 2026 session was quiet for condo and HOA law. The largest community association bill, HB 657 (2026), passed the House but died in the Senate Rules Committee on March 13, 2026. None of its proposals became law, including HOA termination, a community-association court program, and changes to official records and electronic ballots. If someone forwards you a headline about it, it did not pass.

Two 2026 laws took effect July 1, 2026:

  • HB 797 (Chapter 2026-168) rewrote Florida's nonprofit corporation law (Chapter 617). Most associations are organized under it. The bill summary lists:

  • revised officer duties ("good faith, with reasonable care");

  • a process for courts to remove directors;

  • updated meeting and notice procedures.

Florida's HOA statute now points to the new conflict-of-interest section, s. 617.0832, when an HOA contracts with a director's business (s. 720.3033(2), F.S.). Ask your association attorney how HB 797 interacts with your bylaws. We'll cover it in more depth in a later issue.

  • HB 803 (Chapter 2026-63) is mostly a building-permit bill, with one HOA provision. An HOA or its architectural review committee may not require you to already have a government building permit before it will review your plans (s. 720.3035(1)(c), F.S.; bill page).

Condo safety deadlines still in force (from SB 4-D, SB 154 and HB 913):

  • Structural Integrity Reserve Study (SIRS): required for residential condo buildings three habitable stories or higher.

  • Owner-controlled associations existing on or before July 1, 2022 had to complete one by December 31, 2025.

  • If your building's milestone inspection is due on or before December 31, 2026, the SIRS may be done alongside it, but "in no event" later than December 31, 2026 (s. 718.112(2)(g), F.S.; DBPR FAQ).

  • Milestone inspections: due by December 31 of the year the building turns 30 (a local agency may require 25, for example near salt water), then every 10 years (s. 553.899(3), F.S.).

  • After a SIRS:

  • The association must give owners a copy, or notice that it's available, within 45 days (s. 718.112(2)(g)11).

  • It must report the SIRS to DBPR through its online account within 45 days of receiving it (DBPR FAQ).

  • Association websites:

  • Condos with 25+ units (non-timeshare) had to post key documents online by January 1, 2026 (DBPR FAQ; s. 718.111(12)(g)).

  • HOAs with 100+ parcels had to do so by January 1, 2025 (s. 720.303(4)(b)).

Coming up:

  • The 2027 regular session starts March 2, 2027. The Florida Constitution starts odd-year sessions on the first Tuesday after the first Monday in March (Art. III, s. 3).

  • After the November 3, 2026 general election, committee assignments for condo and HOA bills may change.

2. How to get involved: attend and speak

You don't need a board seat to have a voice.

  • Condo board meetings:

  • Open to all owners whenever a quorum of the board is present.

  • You have the right to speak on all designated agenda items and to record the meeting.

  • Notice with a specific agenda must be posted at least 48 continuous hours in advance, except in emergencies.

  • In condos with more than 10 units, the board must meet at least quarterly, and at least four times a year the agenda must include time for owners' questions (s. 718.112(2)(c)).

  • HOA board meetings: open to members, who may speak on all designated items. Notice must be posted 48 hours ahead, or mailed 7 days ahead (s. 720.303(2)).

  • HOA membership meetings: members may speak at least 3 minutes on any item. The association may adopt reasonable rules on how (s. 720.306(6)).

This week's action: find where your association posts meeting notices (the board must designate a location by rule) and put the next board meeting on your calendar.

3. Running for your board: the condo calendar

If your condo's annual election is in early 2027, the timeline starts soon (s. 718.112(2)(d)):

  • 60 days before: the association sends the first notice of the election date.

  • 40 days before: your written notice of intent to run must be received by the association.

  • 35 days before: last day to submit an optional one-page candidate information sheet, which the association mails with the ballot.

  • 14–34 days before: the second notice and ballot go out.

  • Eligibility:

  • You can't run if you're delinquent in any assessment, or have been suspended or removed by the Division.

  • People convicted of a felony are ineligible unless their civil rights have been restored for at least 5 years.

  • Co-owners of one unit generally can't serve at the same time (with exceptions).

  • A director generally can't serve more than 8 consecutive years without a two-thirds vote.

  • At least 20% of eligible voters must cast ballots for the election to be valid.

Next issue: the education and certification every new director must complete.
